messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Graphic Designer
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 40

He is 41, a South Asian man who has built a careful life around color, layout, and control. He works as a graphic designer for a marketing firm, the kind of person who notices when text is one pixel off center or when a shade of blue is almost, but not quite, right. He is married, soft-spoken, and by the time he talks about what happened, it is clear that he has spent years trying to make his inner world look more orderly than it feels.

The event begins on an ordinary weekday evening about two years ago. He stays late at the office finishing a client presentation and leaves after dark, laptop in his backpack, mind still turning over fonts and campaign images. On the drive home, he is pulled over by police for what he assumes is a minor traffic issue. He remembers lowering the window and reaching for his wallet when everything changes quickly. The officer’s tone sharpens. Another patrol car arrives. He is told to step out of the vehicle. He tries to ask what is happening, but the questions seem to make things worse. He recalls seeing one officer’s hand near his weapon and feeling, in an instant, that he might not get home alive.

He says the fear is not abstract. It is physical and total. His mouth goes dry. His hands shake so badly he worries any movement will be misread. He is pushed against the car, searched, and handcuffed on the side of the road while passing drivers slow down to watch. He hears himself saying, “I work nearby, I’m just going home,” as if that should explain his existence, as if being educated, employed, married, harmless might protect him. Later he learns they are looking for someone else. There is no apology that matches the humiliation. He is released and allowed to leave, but he drives home in a daze, gripping the wheel so tightly his fingers cramp.

That night he does not tell the story straight through. He gives his wife fragments. He says there was a misunderstanding, that the police were aggressive, that he is fine. But he does not sleep. Every time he starts to drift off, he is back on the roadside with bright lights in his eyes and a voice ordering him not to move. For weeks he wakes abruptly, heart pounding, sometimes already out of bed before he fully knows where he is.

At first he tells himself it will pass. Instead, his world begins to narrow. He changes his route to avoid the street where it happened. Then he starts avoiding driving after dark altogether. If he sees a police car behind him, even several lanes away, his chest tightens and his thoughts scatter. He checks his mirrors compulsively. He rehearses what he would say if stopped again, then criticizes himself for sounding guilty in his own imaginary script. He becomes hyperaware of his hands, his posture, his tone of voice, as though the smallest mistake could again become dangerous.

At work, the effects show up in ways that confuse him. He has always relied on sustained concentration, but now his attention snaps easily. A siren outside the office pulls him out of a meeting so completely that he cannot follow the conversation for several minutes. He stares at a blank artboard, unable to begin, while his body feels as if it is bracing for impact. Tight deadlines that used to energize him now leave him irritable and flooded. Coworkers notice he startles when someone comes up behind his desk. He laughs it off, but afterward he feels ashamed and exposed.

His wife experiences him as increasingly distant. Before, he used to unwind by cooking with her, discussing movies, or showing her draft concepts from work. Now he comes home and scans the street before getting out of the car. He checks that the front door is locked more than once. When she asks what he is thinking, he often says, “Nothing,” because what he is thinking feels too difficult to explain: the officer’s voice, the pressure of the hood against his cheek, the certainty that his life could be ended in the space of a misunderstanding. He avoids talking about the incident because even naming it makes his skin prickle and his stomach drop.

He also finds himself changed in ways that trouble him. He used to see himself as patient and measured; now anger comes quickly, especially when he feels watched, questioned, or cornered. Small frustrations—a car tailing him, a knock at the door, a stranger lingering too long near him—provoke an outsized reaction. At the same time, part of him has gone numb. He describes moving through some days as if behind glass, able to complete tasks but not fully inhabit them.

In the present, he remains functional from the outside. He meets deadlines, pays bills, answers emails, and sits beside his wife at family gatherings. But his life is organized around anticipation of threat. He notices police uniforms before he notices faces. He studies exits in every public space. Sleep is light and easily broken. He keeps telling himself that nothing is happening now, that he is safe, yet his body does not seem to believe him. What stays with him most is not only the memory of being stopped, but the enduring sense that ordinary life can rupture without warning, and that he can never again move through the world with the same easy assumption of safety.
